In mammalian cells, polyphosphate promotes stress-induced P-body assembly by directly binding the Lsm1–7 heptameric complex or the Edc4 scaffold protein, thereby lowering their saturation concentration for liquid–liquid phase separation, and disrupting predicted polyP-binding basic residues in these proteins will specifically impair P-body formation without affecting stress granules.

Hfq separation-of-function mutants that retain canonical sRNA-mRNA chaperone activity but cannot bind polyphosphate will fail to form nitrogen starvation-induced H-bodies and will phenocopy Δhfq in impaired survival and delayed recovery, demonstrating that polyphosphate-dependent phase separation is the Hfq function required for stress resilience.

An Escherichia coli Hfq mutant engineered to disrupt polyphosphate binding will retain canonical small RNA–mRNA chaperone activity yet fail to form H-bodies, stabilize polyadenylated transcripts, and support survival during nitrogen starvation, thereby phenocopying the Δppk mutant.

Long-chain polyphosphate directly scaffolds the LSm1–7 complex in mammalian cells, lowering its saturation concentration for phase separation and thereby nucleating P-body formation during arsenite-induced stress.
